title: Synchronization in coherently and dissipatively coupled spinor polariton time crystals
authors: I. Carraro-Haddad, A. Ramos-Pérez, G. Usaj, A. Bruchhausen, K. Biermann, P. V. Santos, A. S. Kuznetsov, A. A. Reynoso, A. Fainstein
abstract: The spinor degree of freedom associated to exciton-polariton condensates can spontaneously self-oscillate breaking time translation symmetry, thus showing a continuous time-crystal (CTC) behavior. An open question in such driven-dissipative and non-linear quantum open systems is what happens when CTCs are brought together to interact. Here we experimentally study polariton condensates in coupled traps, evidencing mutual induction and synchronization of the pseudospin temporal GHz dynamics in the CTC phase. The individual and relative orientation of the (limit cycle) precessing pseudospins can be tuned by the optical excitation power, displaying both ferro and anti-ferro dynamical configurations. We theoretically show that the exciton reservoir, and both the coherent and long-range dissipative inter-trap coupling, play important roles in the CTC dynamics. The investigation of time-broken symmetry is thus extended here to more complex non-hermitian systems opening the path to study self-sustained collective dynamics in lattices of non-linear quantum condensates.
summary: This paper explores the synchronization phenomena in coupled spinor polariton condensates exhibiting Continuous Time Crystal behavior. By combining experiments on patterned microcavities with detailed theoretical modeling, the authors show that mutual induction and frequency locking can be achieved through various coupling channels, including dissipation and optomechanics. This extends the understanding of time-broken symmetry to complex, open quantum systems.
main_problem: The study investigates how Continuous Time Crystals (CTCs) synchronize when multiple, coherently or dissipatively coupled spinor polariton condensates interact.
main_result: Synchronization of the pseudospin temporal dynamics is experimentally and theoretically demonstrated, showing that coupling mechanisms—including coherent tunneling, dissipation, and optomechanics—can induce collective time-periodic order.
method: The research combines experimental measurements using spectrally resolved photoluminescence (PL) imaging and time-resolved coherence function analysis with theoretical modeling based on generalized spinor Gross-Pitaevskii equations.
model_or_system: The system involves spinor exciton-polaritons confined in engineered microcavity traps. The dynamics are modeled by coupling the polariton condensate evolution, an exciton reservoir rate equation, and optionally, a mechanical oscillator mode.
key_observables: Pseudospin precession frequency ($\Delta s$), relative integrated intensity ratio, first-order coherence function $g^{(1)}(\mathbf{r}, 	au)$, and spectral line splitting.
important_parameters:
Optical excitation power ($P_{cw}$), inter-trap detuning ($\Delta\epsilon$), coupling strengths (coherent $J_{12}$ vs. dissipative $J_{12,d}$), and the mechanical frequency ($
u_M$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes that the system can be described by coupled non-Hermitian dynamics incorporating reservoir effects and optomechanical back-action.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate spectral evolution (line splitting) vs. power, time-resolved coherence functions showing frequency locking to mechanical modes, and theoretical comparisons between synchronization induced by coherent versus dissipative coupling mechanisms.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from observing basic CTC behavior in single/coupled traps to systematically analyzing the role of different coupling terms—dissipative, coherent, and optomechanical—in achieving robust synchronization across multiple coupled quantum systems.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it tackles non-Hermitian dynamics and time-symmetry breaking in a controllable solid-state platform (polaritons), providing concrete examples of how collective order emerges from complex coupling mechanisms.
